planting.note: Sow after last frost once soil has warmed above 65°F; drill or broadcast into a well-prepared seedbed for maximum biomass production before mowing or grazing.

directions: Drill seed 3/4–1 inch deep into warm, fertile soil in full sun; forage sorghum grows taller and leafier than grain sorghum or sorghum-sudangrass hybrids, commonly reaching 8–15 feet, and is grown specifically for maximum tonnage as silage, green chop, or hay rather than grain or a fast-terminating cover. It is deeply drought-tolerant once established thanks to an extensive root system, making it valuable for building organic matter and suppressing weeds in hot, dry summer conditions where many other warm-season cover crops struggle. Mow or graze at 3–4 feet to encourage tillering and repeated cutting, and allow several weeks for the heavy residue to break down before planting a following crop into it. Note that young, frost-stressed, or drought-stunted sorghum can accumulate prussic acid (cyanogenic compounds) and should not be grazed immediately after a frost or severe drought stress — wait several days and check tissue before turning out livestock.
sources: Midwest Cover Crops Council field guide
Oklahoma State University Extension — Forage Sorghum Production

planting.note: Broadcast scarified seed on a firm, well-prepared seedbed in early to mid spring; sericea lespedeza establishes slowly in its first year but forms a deep-rooted, long-lived stand once settled. It spreads readily by reseeding and can become difficult to remove — plant only where a persistent, deep-rooted legume is genuinely wanted, and check local status before planting, as some states regulate it as a noxious weed.

directions: Broadcast scarified, inoculated seed on a firm seedbed in full sun; extremely drought-tolerant and well adapted to poor, acidic, eroded, or infertile soils once its deep taproot is established. Sericea lespedeza is a warm-season perennial legume long used across the South for erosion control on cut slopes and marginal land, as a nitrogen-fixing soil builder, and as wildlife food-plot forage valued by deer, quail, and turkey for its late-summer seed and leguminous browse. Its deep root system makes it exceptionally drought-hardy and long persisting once established, continuing to produce for a decade or more without reseeding on a well-managed site. Because it spreads aggressively by seed and can outcompete native vegetation in unmanaged settings, it is best confined to dedicated forage or reclamation plantings rather than mixed cover-crop rotations, and mowing before seed set helps limit unwanted spread. Zone 5–9.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Sericea Lespedeza

planting.note: Broadcast or drill 6–10 weeks before the first fall frost into a well-prepared seedbed; oilseed radish grows quickly and, in USDA zone 5 and colder, reliably winter-kills, leaving surface residue and a decomposing root channel by spring.

directions: Broadcast seed at 8–12 lb/acre and lightly incorporate into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; oilseed radish germinates and grows rapidly, producing a vigorous rosette of large leaves over a long, thick taproot. Bred as a fast-biomass, high-glucosinolate type within the same species as tillage/forage radish, it is especially valued for biofumigation — as the roots and residue break down, they release natural sulfur compounds that can suppress certain soilborne pathogens and nematodes, in addition to the physical benefits of a deep taproot that fractures compacted soil layers and scavenges leachable nitrogen before winter. In mild-winter climates the rosette can survive and bolt in spring; mow before flowering to prevent an unwanted seed bank. The decomposing roots produce a strong sulfurous smell for a week or two after a hard freeze — this is normal and passes as residue breaks down.
sources: Midwest Cover Crops Council field guide

planting.note: Drill or broadcast in early fall 4–8 weeks before the first hard frost so plants establish a strong rosette before winter; winter canola overwinters as a low rosette and resumes rapid growth and flowering in spring, typically terminated or harvested in late spring.

directions: Drill seed 1/2–1 inch deep into a firm, fertile seedbed in full sun; establish well before hard frost, since a strong rosette is essential for winter survival. Canola is a low-erucic-acid cultivated form of Brassica napus, grown both as an oilseed cash crop and as a deep-taprooted cover crop that scavenges nitrogen, breaks up compacted subsoil, and adds substantial organic matter ahead of a following summer crop. In spring, the overwintered rosette bolts rapidly and produces tall stems topped with abundant small yellow flowers that are highly attractive to honeybees and other pollinators during an otherwise thin nectar period, making it a valuable dual-purpose planting for growers interested in both soil building and pollinator forage. Terminate by mowing, rolling, or incorporation before or at flowering if grown strictly as a cover crop, since the residue becomes fibrous and slow to break down once the plant sets seed. Zone 5–9.
sources: Midwest Cover Crops Council field guide
Oklahoma State University Extension — Winter Canola Production

planting.note: Scarify seed and broadcast or drill in spring into a firm, well-prepared seedbed in full sun; Illinois bundleflower establishes slowly in its first year while building a deep taproot, then persists as a long-lived perennial stand for many years.

directions: Sow scarified, inoculated seed in a firm seedbed in full sun; drought-tolerant once established thanks to a deep taproot, and tolerant of a wide range of soils including heavier clays. Illinois bundleflower is a native tallgrass prairie legume valued in restoration seed mixes, pasture improvement, and wildlife food plots for its combination of nitrogen fixation, high forage protein content, and excellent seed production — the distinctive round, bristly seed clusters (which give the plant its common name) are heavily used by upland game birds and songbirds through fall and winter. Fine, fern-like, mimosa-type foliage and small white puffball flowers in summer make it an attractive addition to a native prairie or pollinator planting as well as a working forage legume, and once established it persists and reseeds reliably for many years without replanting. A useful, multi-purpose native perennial for pasture, restoration, or wildlife plantings in zone 4–9.
sources: USDA NRCS Plant Fact Sheet — Illinois Bundleflower
